Lessons.Title: Multi-step Conversion Problems: Customary Length
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: sort and compare inches, feet and yards, then solve multi-step customary-length stories involving a rectangular field's perimeter and a whole number of laps compared with a mile. The source first lets learners sort measurement cards by any justified grouping and then requires matching equivalent physical lengths.

Warm-up: measure or describe a one-yard stick with three feet and36 inches. Explain why a number such as72 inches describes the same distance as6 feet or2 yards and why a larger printed count does not mean a longer object.

Activity 1 — first-party card equivalents: match 2 yards=6 feet=72 inches, 2 1/2 yards=7 1/2 feet=90 inches, and3 yards=9 feet=108 inches. Sort the representations both by unit form and by exact physical length, then order the groups from shortest to longest. Teacher reviews alternate valid classification criteria.

Activity 2 — perimeter and mile: original rectangular field100 yards long by48 1/2 yards wide has perimeter2×(100+48 1/2)=297 yards. Six laps equal1782 yards, which is22 yards MORE than one mile (1760 yards). For another field90 by55 yards, perimeter290 yards; twelve laps cover3480 yards, short of two miles (3520 yards), while thirteen cover3770, so13 full laps are required to reach at least two miles.

Teacher boundary: the card-sort criteria, diagrams of a field and interpretation of a whole lap cannot be certified by a numeric converter; source asks students to critique a claim, state units and defend a minimum count. Original card images and protected teacher responses not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Customary length relations
KeyConcepts.Definition: One yard equals three feet equals36 inches; one mile equals5280 feet or1760 yards.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rectangular perimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two laps over each pair of perpendicular sides form a rectangle's perimeter.

KeyConcepts.Title: Minimum whole laps
KeyConcepts.Definition: For 'at least' a distance, use the smallest whole number of complete laps whose product meets the target.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match length cards
WorkedExamples.Question: Match2.5yd with feet and inches.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.
Steps: Multiply2.5 by3 to convert to feet.
Multiply feet by12 to convert to inches.
Explain all three values describe one length.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare six laps with a mile
WorkedExamples.Question: A field is100yd by48.5yd. Do six perimeter laps exceed one mile?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two-mile minimum
WorkedExamples.Question: A 90-by-55-yard field has290-yard perimeter. How many whole laps reach at least two miles?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.
Steps: Try12 laps, equal3480 yards, which is insufficient.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 5280 describes FEET per mile, not yards.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use1760 yards per mile or divide feet by3.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Round down a required lap count
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A partial lap quotient does not meet the 'whole laps at least' requirement.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check successive integers against the target and round up if needed.

SummaryPoints: Convert and compare customary lengths with compatible units.
Perimeter and whole-lap repetition require different operations.
Teacher reviews card-sort criteria, diagrams and minimum-lap argument.

Lessons.Title: Add and Subtract Fractions PLC Activity
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: add and subtract fraction quantities when denominators match or differ by inventing categories for an expression-card sort, then using diagrams, equal parts or equivalent fractions in any mathematically defensible way. The source explicitly permits multiple grouping rationales and does not require formal common-denominator rules as the only entry point.

Warm-up: compare one half with two fourths using a single fixed-unit tape. Both shade the same length and have different numerator/denominator pairs; explain why they can be combined after renaming one or both.

Activity 1 — category sort: first-party expressions 3/4+1/2,3/4+3/4,3/4−1/8,2/5+3/10 and5/6−1/3 may be grouped by same versus different denominators, by addition versus subtraction, or by whether the result exceeds one. At least two valid classification systems and student explanations are required.

Activity 2 — find three values: 3/4+3/4=6/4=1 1/2 by adding identical fourths; 3/4−1/8=6/8−1/8=5/8 by eighth strips; 3/4+1/2=3/4+2/4=5/4=1 1/4 by common quarters. Different number-line or tape-diagram strategies must refer to the same unit whole.

Assessment: the original task asks learners to explain their own sort, change categories and choose strategies. A single automated arithmetic answer cannot certify card sorting, drawn partitions, partner comparison or multiple valid methods.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal denominators represent same-size parts
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fractions with common denominators can add or subtract their part counts.
KeyConcepts.Example: The result can exceed one whole.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fractions for unlike denominators
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rename each fraction in equal parts of a consistent whole before combining.

KeyConcepts.Title: Flexible expression grouping
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction card may be grouped by operation, denominator relationship or result size.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 3/4+3/4 is addition with like denominators AND a sum above one.
KeyConcepts.Example: Teacher reviews a meaningful second classification.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same denominator
WorkedExamples.Question: Find3/4+3/4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.
Steps: Keep one whole divided into fourths.
Regroup four quarters as one whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Subtract unlike parts
WorkedExamples.Question: Find3/4−1/8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Add halves to quarters
WorkedExamples.Question: Find3/4+1/2.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.
Steps: Add three and two equal fourths.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The sum must count equal-sized portions, not create an arbitrary new unit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Rename both terms with a common denominator, then add numerators.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim a single correct card classification
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Several grouping criteria can be justified from exact mathematical properties.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the rule for each classification and ensure all cards actually satisfy it.

SummaryPoints: Fractions can be added or subtracted with diagrams or equivalent unit parts.
Different card-sort explanations are legitimate when clearly justified.
Teacher review is needed for drawing and categorization.

Lessons.Title: Use Equivalent Expressions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: identify several equivalent fraction sums/differences and strategically choose a common denominator, sometimes simplifying before adding. The 2021 source asks why alternative expressions are equivalent, then compares different decompositions for differences and optionally a plant-growth story with unlike fractions.
Warm-up: a fraction such as 3/4 can be described as6/8 or9/12 because the count and size of parts change together. Explain why multiplying just the numerator produces a different quantity.

Activity 1 — same sum with different units: find 2/3+5/12. Convert2/3=8/12 to obtain13/12=1 1/12. Alternatively work in sixths and twelfths as needed, showing that equivalent forms preserve the original total. Describe why twelfths are convenient without insisting they are the only denominator.

Activity 2 — subtract and compare: find 5/4−1/2 as5/4−2/4=3/4, or rewrite 5/4=15/12 and1/2=6/12 for9/12=3/4. A plant example using hypothetical growth1 5/8 inches versus3/4 inch gives a difference of7/8 inch; a student can add on or subtract after renaming.

Teacher boundary: source requires matching equivalences, explaining numerator-and-denominator transformations, and comparing partner strategies. Numeric fractions alone do not prove the learner understood why a new expression is equivalent.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fraction identity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same nonzero integer preserves fraction value.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choose a helpful common denominator
KeyConcepts.Definition: A denominator that both original denominators divide evenly allows comparison of same-sized parts.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mixed fraction differences
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mixed fraction can be changed to an improper fraction or compared with another fraction by adding on.

WorkedExamples.Title: Equivalent fraction sum
WorkedExamples.Question: Find2/3+5/12.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.
Steps: Regroup13/12 into one whole and a twelfth.

WorkedExamples.Title: Equivalent difference
WorkedExamples.Question: Find5/4−1/2 in fourths and twelfths.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.
WorkedExamples.Check: Two different denominator choices yield same value.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare growth
WorkedExamples.Question: A fictional plant grows1 5/8in and another grows3/4in. How much more grew the first?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Change a denominator without scaling the numerator
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That changes fraction size and gives non-equivalent expressions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use the same multiplier on numerator and denominator.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume a larger common denominator always makes calculations easier
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An unnecessarily large common denominator can complicate arithmetic.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare common multiples and simplify when useful.

SummaryPoints: Equivalent expressions support accurate addition and subtraction of unlike denominators.
Several common denominators may be valid, with efficiency a separate criterion.
Teacher reviews equivalence explanations, not only a fraction answer.

Lessons.Title: All Sorts of Denominators
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: explain why multiplying two denominators always produces SOME common denominator, then choose a smaller or more useful common multiple when available. The source contrasts using a guaranteed product with spotting an easier common unit, and asks children to justify both the method and their actual sum/difference.

Warm-up: compare the common denominator 24 for3/4+2/3 with the smaller denominator12. Both are mathematically sound, but 12 produces smaller equivalent numerators than24. Explain why multiplying4×3=12 always supplies a multiple of both.

Activity 1 — new sums: find3/8+2/5 using40ths, giving15/40+16/40=31/40. Find7/10−2/3 using30ths, giving21/30−20/30=1/30. Students can draw area bars, use multiplicative equivalence, or explain part counts.

Activity 2 — choose between denominators: 2/3+5/9 can use9ths to give6/9+5/9=11/9, or27ths to give18/27+15/27=33/27=11/9. Discuss why both work, and why the least common denominator is often more convenient while the denominator product is a guaranteed fallback.

Assessment: teacher reviews a proof of denominator product as a common multiple, correct equivalences and a rationale for choice. Merely outputting31/40 is a small algorithmic subskill of the original source task.

KeyConcepts.Title: Product denominator always works
KeyConcepts.Definition: For positive denominators b and d, bd is divisible by both b and d.

KeyConcepts.Title: Smaller common multiple can be simpler
KeyConcepts.Definition: A common denominator need not be the least, but smaller equivalent counts are often easier.

KeyConcepts.Title: Like-unit subtraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: Common denominators let numerators count same-size parts.

WorkedExamples.Title: Different denominators with no simple multiple
WorkedExamples.Question: Find3/8+2/5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Subtract with thirtieths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find7/10−2/3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.
Steps: Interpret one part in the original whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Contrast 9 versus 27
WorkedExamples.Question: Find2/3+5/9 with two common denominators.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume the product of denominators is the only valid common denominator
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Any shared positive multiple works, including a smaller common multiple.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Consider easy multiples before multiplying denominators.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Multiply denominator factors but forget the numerator conversions
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Changing partition sizes requires changing selected counts proportionally.
CommonMistakes.Correction: For a/b to denominator bd, multiply numerator by d too.

SummaryPoints: The denominator product gives a guaranteed common unit, not always the best unit.
Like-unit arithmetic can use any valid common multiple with numerator scaling.
Teacher reviews explanation of why the algorithm works and method selection.

Lessons.Title: Different Ways to Subtract
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: subtract unlike-denominator mixed numbers and select among decomposition, regrouping and adding-on strategies, explaining why an equivalent mixed-number form can make a tricky fractional subtraction possible. The source deliberately uses fractions close to a whole and has students compare work in a gallery display.
Warm-up: rename 4 1/4 as3 5/4 and as17/4; all are the same amount, but the second mixed expression permits subtracting a larger fractional part. Identify when borrowing one whole is useful.

Activity 1 — justify regrouping: calculate4 1/4−2 5/6. Rewrite4 1/4 as3 15/12, because4 1/4=3+15/12; 2 5/6=2+10/12. Subtract corresponding whole and twelfth parts to yield1+5/12=1 5/12. Compare to directly computing17/4−17/6=17/12. The original whole stays fixed.

Activity 2 — count up for close mixed numbers: 5 1/8−4 7/8 can be found by adding1/8 to4 7/8 to get5, then1/8 more to5 1/8, total1/4. Another 3 2/3−1 5/6 can be found with sixths: 22/6−11/6=11/6=1 5/6. Ask learners which approach is clearest and why.

Assessment: source asks for selecting equivalences, a valid diagram, a reasoned method choice, and comparison of gallery displays; a numeric answer does not verify those student-generated reasoning tasks. Protected source graphics and gated response not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Regroup one whole in a mixed number
KeyConcepts.Definition: One whole can be exchanged for denominator-many fractional pieces to make a subtraction possible.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common units in mixed difference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rewrite fractions as equal-sized parts before subtracting.

KeyConcepts.Title: Adding on
KeyConcepts.Definition: The gap between near-whole mixed numbers can be counted by short forward steps.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use regrouping
WorkedExamples.Question: Find4 1/4−2 5/6.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.
Steps: Exchange one whole from4 to get3 15/12.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use counting up
WorkedExamples.Question: Find5 1/8−4 7/8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.

WorkedExamples.Title: Subtract in sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find3 2/3−1 5/6.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party fraction or measurement representation with exact arithmetic check and teacher-scored reasoning.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Subtract the smaller fraction from a larger fraction while ignoring the borrow
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A mixed fractional part can be smaller than the fraction being removed.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Exchange one whole for fractional parts or use improper fractions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count mixed number gaps with inconsistent partition units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Adding eighths to sixths requires compatible fractional units if done in one calculation.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a common denominator, or separate whole-unit jumps with properly labeled fractional distances.

SummaryPoints: Mixed-number subtraction can be shown with regrouped equivalents or adding on.
Any valid strategy must preserve the whole and use compatible units.
Teacher reviews strategy choice and mathematical explanations.
